member.name: T:GtkSystem.Resources.Extensions.DeserializingResourceReader
member.summary: DeserializingResourceReader is a class that provides an implementation of deserializing a resource file. It reads resources from a stream and allows access to them through the IResourceReader interface. The class supports both binary formatted resources and resources that use type converters for serialization. It also includes error handling to ensure that the resource file is properly formatted and that the resources can be deserialized correctly.

member.name: T:GtkSystem.Resources.Extensions.PreserializedResourceWriter
member.summary: PreserializedResourceWriter is a class that implements the IResourceWriter interface and is used to write resources to a stream or file in a pre-serialized format. It allows for adding resources of various types, including strings, byte arrays, and streams, and handles the serialization of these resources in a way that can be read by a corresponding resource reader. The class also manages the underlying stream and ensures that all resources are properly written and the stream is closed when done.

member.name: T:GtkSystem.Resources.ResourceManager
member.summary: ResourceManager is a class that provides convenient access to culture-specific resources at runtime. It enables you to retrieve resources based on the current culture or a specified culture. This class is typically used in applications that support multiple languages and cultures, allowing you to manage and access localized resources such as strings, images, and other data.

member.summary: Gets the value of the specified non-string resource localized for the specified culture.
member.param: The name of the resource to get.

The culture for which the resource is localized. If the resource is not localized for this culture, the resource manager uses fallback rules to locate an appropriate resource. If this value is null, the
object is obtained by using the
property.
member.returns:
The value of the resource, localized for the specified culture. If an appropriate resource set exists but

member.remarks: The culture used to be discarded outright - every culture-qualified lookup resolved to the neutral resource, so a localized .resx could never win. It now walks the standard fallback chain.

member.name: T:GtkSystem.Windows.Forms.GtkControls.ControlBase.GtkControlOverride
member.summary:
GtkControlOverride is a class that provides an implementation of the IControlOverride interface for GTK controls. It allows developers to customize the appearance and behavior of GTK controls by providing properties for background color, background image, image layout, and image alignment. The class also includes methods for adding and removing CSS classes, clearing native backgrounds, and handling drawing events for the control's background and images. By using GtkControlOverride, developers can easily enhance the visual aspects of their GTK controls while maintaining compatibility with the underlying GTK framework.
GtkControlOverride is a reusable helper attached to GTK widget wrappers to centralize painting, background/image handling and CSS-class management. It’s constructed by controls (in their constructors), then the control calls its lifecycle helpers from GTK overrides. Where it’s created(examples in your repo) What GtkControlOverride provides / how it’s used • Construction: pass the GTK Widget instance to the ctor: new GtkControlOverride(widget). • CSS management: AddClass(string) / RemoveClass(string) and OnAddClass() applies the list to container.StyleContext. • Background handling: • BackColor, BackgroundImage, BackgroundImageLayout properties control background painting. • OnDrawnBackground(Cairo.Context, Gdk.Rectangle) paints the BackColor and scaled background image, then raises DrawnBackground. • Foreground/image painting: • Image / ImageAlign for a displayed image; OnDrawnImage(...) draws it. • Paint events: • OnPaint(Cairo.Context, Gdk.Rectangle) raises: • PaintGraphics(Cairo.Context, Rectangle) — for direct Cairo drawing callbacks. • Paint(object, PaintEventArgs) — for System.Drawing-style painting; it builds a Graphics wrapper and passes it in PaintEventArgs. • ClearNativeBackground() is present as a hook(empty by default) for platform-specific background clearing. Typical usage pattern in a control • Create override in your control constructor. • Add style classes with Override.AddClass(...). • In the control’s GTK draw handler call: • Override.OnDrawnBackground(cr, area) — to paint background and image, or • Override.OnDrawnImage(cr, area) — to paint the image. • In OnDrawn(Cairo.Context) you can call Override.OnPaint(cr, area) to raise Paint/PaintGraphics for custom drawing.

member.name: M:System.Windows.Forms.BindingManagerBase.OnBindingsCollectionChanged(System.Object,System.ComponentModel.CollectionChangeEventArgs)
member.summary:
BindingComplete events on individual Bindings are propagated up through the BindingComplete event on the owning BindingManagerBase. To do this, we have to track changes to the bindings collection, adding or removing handlers on items in the collection as appropriate.
For the Add and Remove cases, we hook the collection 'changed' event, and add or remove handler for specific binding.
For the Refresh case, we hook both the 'changing' and 'changed' events, removing handlers for all items that were in the collection before the change, then adding handlers for whatever items are in the collection after the change.

member.name: T:System.Windows.Forms.Control
member.summary: Represents the collection of data bindings for a control.
Represents the collection of data bindings for a control.

Keyboard-command routing, right-to-left alignment translation and parent-change notification override points that custom controls ported from WinForms rely on. These mirror the real System.Windows.Forms.Control members so overriding source compiles and behaves.
The dock/anchor arrangement pass — WinForms' DefaultLayout arithmetic, run over the GTK children of a container.

remarks.para: Dock and anchor used to be expressed by handing each child a GTK alignment: a top-docked child was given Halign=Fill, Valign=Start, and that was that. GTK then aligned every such child to the same edge, so two top-docked panels landed on top of each other instead of stacking, and covered the whole container rather than what was left of it. Anchoring was computed once when the widget was realized and never again, so resizing the container moved nothing.

WinForms instead computes child rectangles itself: docked children consume edges of a shrinking remainder, in reverse order of the control collection, and anchored children follow the container's size delta. That arithmetic is reproduced here and pushed to GTK as absolute margins with Align.Start, so the widget tree carries positions rather than alignment rules.
The expected values are not invented: they were taken from real System.Windows.Forms for the same layouts, and the cases are pinned in LayoutArrangementFunctionalTests.

member.summary: The bounds-core, scaling and handle-lifecycle override surface. These are the protected methods a custom control overrides to intercept sizing, DPI/font scaling and handle recreation; they were absent, so class MyControl : Control { protected override void SetBoundsCore(...) } did not compile.

Non-rectangular control shapes - Control.Region. The property existed as an inert auto-property: assigning it stored a region and shaped nothing, so a shaped control (a round button, a skinned splash form) compiled, ran, and stayed rectangular.
Represents the collection of data bindings for a control.

member.name: M:System.Windows.Forms.Control.WndProc(System.Windows.Forms.Message@)
member.summary: Processes a Windows message for the control (placeholder).
member.remarks: There is no Win32 message pump behind this library, so nothing ever feeds this method. It used to have an empty body, which meant an override intended to intercept WM_NCHITTEST, WM_ERASEBKGND, drag-move or non-client painting compiled cleanly and then silently did nothing at run time. Throwing states the boundary instead of hiding it: message interception is a documented non-goal, not an unfinished feature. Use the WinForms event model (OnPaint, OnMouseDown, HitTest and so on), which is fully wired.

member.remarks: Not supported for the same reason as .

member.name: P:System.Windows.Forms.Control.Region
member.summary: Gets or sets the window region associated with the control.
member.value: The that represents the window region, in client coordinates, or for the whole rectangle.
member.remarks:
Backed by GTK's shape-combine, which - like the Win32 window region this mirrors - takes a list of rectangles. A region whose interior is a real path is therefore applied as the rectangles it decomposes into, so a curved outline is stepped at pixel resolution rather than smooth. That is what Win32 does too; the difference is only how finely the curve is scanned.
The shape needs a realized widget, so a region assigned before the handle exists is remembered and applied when the widget is realized.
**Substrate limit.** A shape lives on a GDK window, and lightweight GTK widgets - buttons, labels, and anything else that draws onto its parent rather than owning a window - do not have one. On those the region is stored and reported but changes nothing. Forms and the container controls ( and friends) do own a window and are shaped for real, which covers the shaped-window and custom-drawn-container cases the property exists for.

member.name: M:System.Windows.Forms.Control.ApplyRegion
member.summary: Pushes down to the widget, or clears the shape when it is . A no-op until the widget is realized - is called again from the realize handler.

member.name: M:System.Windows.Forms.Control.ToCairoRegion(System.Drawing.Region)
member.summary: Converts a to the pixel-rectangle region GTK's shape-combine takes.
member.returns: when is or covers everything - which is how the shape is reset - otherwise the region's rectangles, rounded outwards so no part of the requested shape is clipped away.

member.name: T:System.Windows.Forms.AccessibleObject
member.summary: Provides information that accessibility applications use to adjust an application's user interface (UI) for users with impairments.
member.remarks:
This was an empty class and always returned null, so the accessibility API was present in name only - nothing reached a screen reader on any platform. It is now backed by the GTK widget's ATK peer, which is what AT-SPI (Orca, and the accessibility bridges on Windows and macOS) actually reads.
Scope: name, description, role, value, bounds and parent/child navigation are wired. The richer UI Automation pattern surface of modern WinForms is not emulated.

member.summary: Gets or sets the dimensions the control was designed against.
member.remarks: This and used to be inert auto-properties on . Every designer-generated form sets them, so a layout produced at one font metric or DPI was never rescaled at another - exactly the case a cross-platform layer hits hardest, because Linux and macOS font metrics differ from those of Windows.

member.summary: The control paints itself; WM_PAINT and WM_ERASEBKGND messages are not passed on to the underlying NativeWindow. This style only applies to subclasses of Control.

member.name: F:System.Windows.Forms.ControlStyles.Opaque
member.summary: If specified, a PaintBackground event will not be raised, OnPaintBackground will not be called, and Invalidate() will not invalidate the background of the HWND.

member.name: F:System.Windows.Forms.ControlStyles.ResizeRedraw
member.summary: The control is completely redrawn when it is resized.

member.name: F:System.Windows.Forms.ControlStyles.FixedWidth
member.summary: The control has a fixed width.

member.name: F:System.Windows.Forms.ControlStyles.FixedHeight
member.summary: The control has a fixed height.

member.name: F:System.Windows.Forms.ControlStyles.StandardClick
member.summary: If set, windows forms calls OnClick and raises the Click event when the control is clicked (unless it's the second click of a double-click and StandardDoubleClick is specified). Regardless of this style, the control may call OnClick directly.

member.name: F:System.Windows.Forms.ControlStyles.Selectable
member.summary: The control can get the focus.

member.name: F:System.Windows.Forms.ControlStyles.UserMouse
member.summary: The control does its own mouse processing; WM_MOUSEDOWN, WM_MOUSEMOVE, and WM_MOUSEUP messages are not passed on to the underlying NativeWindow.

member.name: F:System.Windows.Forms.ControlStyles.SupportsTransparentBackColor
member.summary: If the BackColor is set to a color whose alpha component is less than 255 (i.e., BackColor.A is less than 255), OnPaintBackground will simulate transparency by asking its parent control to paint our background. This is not true transparency -- if there is another control between us and our parent, we will not show the control in the middle. This style only applies to subclasses of Control. It only works if UserPaint is set, and the parent control is a Control.

member.name: F:System.Windows.Forms.ControlStyles.StandardDoubleClick
member.summary: If set, windows forms calls OnDoubleClick and raises the DoubleClick event when the control is double clicked. Regardless of whether it is set, the control may call OnDoubleClick directly. This style is ignored if StandardClick is not set.

member.name: F:System.Windows.Forms.ControlStyles.AllPaintingInWmPaint
member.summary: If true, WM_ERASEBKGND is ignored, and both OnPaintBackground and OnPaint are called directly from WM_PAINT. This generally reduces flicker, but can cause problems if other controls send WM_ERASEBKGND messages to us. (This is sometimes done to achieve a pseudo-transparent effect similar to ControlStyles.SupportsTransparentBackColor; for instance, ToolBar with flat appearance does this). This style only makes sense if UserPaint is true.

member.name: F:System.Windows.Forms.ControlStyles.CacheText
member.summary: If true, the control keeps a copy of the text rather than going to the hWnd for the text every time. This improves performance but makes it difficult to keep the control and hWnd's text synchronized. This style defaults to false.

member.name: F:System.Windows.Forms.ControlStyles.EnableNotifyMessage
member.summary: If true, the OnNotifyMessage method will be called for every message sent to the control's WndProc. This style defaults to false.

member.name: F:System.Windows.Forms.ControlStyles.DoubleBuffer
member.summary: If set, all control painting will be double buffered. You must also set the UserPaint and AllPaintingInWmPaint style. Note: This is obsolete, please use OptimizedDoubleBuffer instead.

member.name: F:System.Windows.Forms.ControlStyles.OptimizedDoubleBuffer
member.summary: If set, all control painting will be double buffered.

member.name: F:System.Windows.Forms.ControlStyles.UseTextForAccessibility
member.summary: If this style is set, and there is a value in the control's Text property, that value will be used to determine the control's default Active Accessibility name and shortcut key. Otherwise, the text of the preceding Label control will be used instead. This style is set by default. Certain built-in control types such as TextBox and ComboBox un-set this style, so that their current text will not be used by Active Accessibility.

member.name: F:System.Windows.Forms.AccessibleEvents.Destroy
member.summary:
EVENT_OBJECT_DESTROY
Sent when an object has been destroyed. The system sends this event for the following user interface elements: caret, header control, list-view control, tab control, toolbar control, tree view control, and window object. Server applications send this event for their accessible objects.

member.name: F:System.Windows.Forms.AccessibleEvents.Show
member.summary:
EVENT_OBJECT_SHOW
Sent when a hidden object is shown. The system sends this event for the following user interface elements: caret, cursor, and window object. Server applications send this event for their accessible objects. Clients assume that when this event is sent by a parent object, all child objects are already displayed. Therefore, server applications do not send this event for the child objects.

member.name: F:System.Windows.Forms.AccessibleEvents.Hide
member.summary:
EVENT_OBJECT_HIDE
Sent when an object is hidden. The system sends this event for the following user interface elements: caret and cursor. Server applications send this event for their accessible objects. When this event is generated for a parent object, all child objects are already hidden. Server applications do not send this event for the child objects.

member.name: F:System.Windows.Forms.AccessibleEvents.Reorder
member.summary:
EVENT_OBJECT_REORDER
Sent when a container object has added, removed, or reordered its children. The system sends this event for the following user interface elements: header control, list-view control, toolbar control, and window object. Server applications send this event as appropriate for their accessible objects.

member.name: F:System.Windows.Forms.AccessibleEvents.Focus
member.summary: Minimize the number of notifications! When you are hiding a parent object, obviously all child objects are no longer visible on screen. They still have the same "visible" status, but are not truly visible. Hence do not send HIDE notifications for the children also. One implies all. The same goes for SHOW.

member.summary: The selection

member.name: F:System.Windows.Forms.AccessibleEvents.SelectionAdd
member.summary: The selection add

member.summary: The selection remove

member.summary: The selection within

member.name: F:System.Windows.Forms.AccessibleEvents.StateChange
member.summary: There is only one "focused" child item in a parent. This is the place keystrokes are going at a given moment. Hence only send a notification about where the NEW focus is going. A NEW item getting the focus already implies that the OLD item is losing it. SELECTION however can be multiple. Hence the different SELECTION notifications. Here's when to use each: (1) Send a SELECTION notification in the simple single selection case (like the focus) when the item with the selection is merely moving to a different item within a container. hwnd + ID is the container control, idChildItem is the new child with the selection. (2) Send a SELECTIONADD notification when a new item has simply been added to the selection within a container. This is appropriate when the number of newly selected items is very small. hwnd + ID is the container control, idChildItem is the new child added to the selection. (3) Send a SELECTIONREMOVE notification when a new item has simply been removed from the selection within a container. This is appropriate when the number of newly selected items is very small, just like SELECTIONADD. hwnd + ID is the container control, idChildItem is the new child removed from the selection. (4) Send a SELECTIONWITHIN notification when the selected items within a control have changed substantially. Rather than propagate a large number of changes to reflect removal for some items, addition of others, just tell somebody who cares that a lot happened. It will be faster an easier for somebody watching to just turn around and query the container control what the new bunch of selected items are.

member.name: F:System.Windows.Forms.AccessibleStates.ExtSelectable
member.summary:
Alters the selection so that all objects between the selection anchor, which is the object with the keyboard focus, and this object take on the anchor object's selection state. If the anchor object is not selected, the objects are removed from the selection. If the anchor object is selected, the selection is extended to include this object and all the objects in between. You can set the selection state by combining this flag with or . This flag does not change the focus or the selection anchor unless it is combined with . The behavior of |
is equivalent to adding an item to a selection manually by holding down the SHIFT key and clicking an unselected object. This flag may not be combined with .

member.name: F:System.Windows.Forms.AccessibleStates.AlertLow
member.summary: Low-priority information that may not be important to the user.

member.name: F:System.Windows.Forms.AccessibleStates.AlertMedium
member.summary: Important information that does not need to be conveyed to the user immediately. For example, when a battery level indicator is starting to reach a low level, it could generate a medium-level alert. Blind access utilities could then generate a sound to let the user know that important information is available, without actually interrupting the user's work. The user could then query the alert information at their leisure.

member.name: F:System.Windows.Forms.AccessibleStates.AlertHigh
member.summary: Important information that should be conveyed to the user immediately. For example, a battery level indicator reaching a critical low level would transition to this state, in which case a blind access utility would announce this information immediately to the user, and a screen magnification program would scroll the screen so that the battery indicator is in view. This state is also appropriate for any prompt or operation that must be completed before the user can continue.

member.name: F:System.Windows.Forms.ImeMode.Disable

member.name: P:System.Windows.Forms.Padding.All
member.summary: Gets or sets the padding value for all the edges.
member.returns: The padding, in pixels, for all edges if the same; otherwise, -1.
member.remarks: This was a stored auto-property that the four-edge constructor set to left, so a Padding with differing edges reported the left edge as if every edge matched it. WinForms computes All, returning -1 when the edges differ; setting it applies the value to every edge.

member.name: P:System.Windows.Forms.Padding.Bottom
member.summary: Gets or sets the padding value for the bottom edge.
member.returns: The padding, in pixels, for the bottom edge.

member.name: P:System.Windows.Forms.Padding.Horizontal
member.summary: Gets the combined padding for the right and left edges.
member.returns: Gets the sum, in pixels, of the System.Windows.Forms.Padding.Left and System.Windows.Forms.Padding.Right padding values.
member.remarks: This computed Right - Left, contradicting its own documentation and WinForms, where Horizontal is the sum of the two edges. Symmetric padding therefore reported 0, so every "client width = Width - Padding.Horizontal" calculation silently used the full width.

member.name: T:System.Windows.Forms.ErrorProvider
member.summary: Provides a user interface for indicating that a control on a form has an error associated with it.
member.remarks:
This type was missing entirely, and it is the standard WinForms validation pattern — almost any data-entry form has one — so its absence was a compile break in very common code.
It is an extender provider of the same shape as : the error text set for a control is stored, reported back by , and surfaced to the user through the control's tooltip, which is what this GTK layer can address reliably. The adjacent blinking icon that WinForms draws in the parent container is not reproduced — placing a floating adornment next to an arbitrary child would need layout surgery in the GTK container model. , and the per-control alignment and padding are stored faithfully so that application code and designer output round-trip, but they do not currently affect rendering.

member.name: T:System.Windows.Forms.Form
member.summary: Represents a window or dialog box that makes up an application's user interface.

The pre-2.0 lifecycle events (, , , ) plus owned-form management, parent-form access, validation and centering. These mirror System.Windows.Forms.Form so source that predates FormClosing/FormClosed — a very common partial surface — keeps compiling and behaving.

Window-placement surface: desktop-relative bounds, the maximize/restore rectangles and right-to-left layout. These were absent, so designer or application code touching DesktopBounds, RestoreBounds, MaximizedBounds or RightToLeftLayout did not compile.
Colour-keyed window transparency - Form.TransparencyKey and Form.AllowTransparency. Neither member existed, so the standard shaped-window idiom (BackColor = X; TransparencyKey = X;) did not compile.

member.name: P:System.Windows.Forms.Form.AllowTransparency
member.summary: Gets or sets a value indicating whether the form can be made transparent - through or .
member.remarks: Assigning a non-empty turns this on, as it does in WinForms. Turning it off clears the key.

member.name: P:System.Windows.Forms.Form.TransparencyKey
member.summary: Gets or sets the colour that will represent transparent areas of the form.
member.value: The colour to treat as transparent, or - the default - for an opaque form.

remarks.para: What is emulated: the idiom this member exists for, a form whose background colour *is* the key, so the window's own background becomes invisible and only the controls on it are drawn. The window is given an RGBA visual and its background is painted with zero alpha.

What is not: per-pixel colour keying of arbitrary content - a key that matches a colour inside a child control or a background image leaves those pixels opaque - and click-through, which in WinForms lets the mouse pass through keyed areas. GTK expresses both through an input shape that would have to be recomputed from the rendered pixels on every paint. Documented deviation.

member.name: P:System.Windows.Forms.Form.IsTransparencySupported
member.summary: Gets a value indicating whether the screen this form is on can actually composite transparency.
member.remarks: There is no WinForms equivalent - on Windows the answer is always yes. It is exposed because on X11 without a compositor, and on some remote sessions, it is no, and a form that silently stays opaque is otherwise indistinguishable from a bug.

member.name: M:System.Windows.Forms.Form.ApplyTransparency
member.summary: Pushes the current transparency settings to the window: an RGBA visual and an alpha-zero background while a key matching the form's own background colour is set, the normal visual and background otherwise.

member.summary: The base class for , and .
member.remarks: The whole legacy menu family was missing. These types are obsolete in modern WinForms, but an application old enough to be worth porting is very likely to use them, so their absence was a hard compile break at the start of a migration rather than a runtime surprise later. They are implemented as adapters over the ToolStrip family, which is what actually renders.

member.name: T:System.Windows.Forms.ToolStripItem
member.summary: Represents the abstract base class that manages events and layout for all the elements that a or can contain.

Common members that ported source references directly — accessibility, selection/placement state and drag flags. They were absent from the surface; because they live on the base they reach every item type (buttons, menu items, labels, the hosted text/combo boxes). They compile and round-trip; the GTK substrate drives the visual placement, so the placement-ish ones are stored settings rather than live layout inputs.

member.name: M:System.Windows.Forms.ClientUtils.GetWordBoundaryStart(System.String,System.Int32)
member.summary: Imitates the backwards word selection logic of the native SHAutoComplete Ctrl+Backspace handler. The selection will consist of any run of word characters and any run of non-word characters at the end of that word. If the selection reaches the second character in the input, and the first character is non-word, it is also selected. Here, word characters are equivalent to the "\w" regex class but with UnicodeCategory.ConnectorPunctuation excluded.

member.name: T:System.Windows.Forms.Splitter
member.summary: Represents a splitter control that lets the user resize docked controls.
member.remarks:
The legacy splitter, distinct from the that replaced it, was missing. An application old enough to be worth porting will very likely dock one of these against a panel, so its absence was a compile break.
It is a docked carrying the legacy surface — the / limits, and the / events — and resizes the control it is docked against when the position changes. Interactive dragging is not wired to GTK input; setting from code performs the resize.

member.name: T:System.Windows.Forms.TextBoxBase
member.summary: Implements the basic functionality required by text controls (, and ). This mirrors the real System.Windows.Forms.TextBoxBase so that source written against the shared editing surface — and type tests such as control is TextBoxBase — compile and behave.
member.remarks:
The concrete text storage differs per control (a GTK entry versus a text view), so the primitives that touch the widget are abstract and supplied by the derived control; the clipboard, undo and modified-state behaviour is implemented once here on top of them.
Undo covers the content-editing operations routed through this class (, , , and setting ). It does not capture individual keystrokes, which GTK handles internally.

member.name: T:System.Windows.Forms.TextRenderer
member.summary: Provides methods used to measure and render text.
member.remarks: This type was missing entirely. TextRenderer.MeasureText / DrawText has been the recommended WinForms text API since .NET 2.0 and appears in a large share of custom-drawn WinForms code, so its absence was a frequent compile break. This implementation measures and draws through , which is backed by Pango, and honours the alignment, single-line and padding bits of .

member.summary: Implements the basic functionality required by a spin box (also known as an up-down control), the shared base of and . member.name: T:System.Windows.Forms.VisualStyles.VisualStyleInformation
member.summary: Provides information about the current visual style of the operating system. On this GTK layer the values reflect the active GTK theme, which is always present, so visual styles are reported as supported and enabled.

member.name: P:System.Windows.Forms.VisualStyles.VisualStyleInformation.IsSupportedByOS
member.summary: Gets a value indicating whether the operating system supports visual styles. Always (GTK themes).

member.name: P:System.Windows.Forms.VisualStyles.VisualStyleInformation.IsEnabledByUser
member.summary: Gets a value indicating whether visual styles are enabled by the user. Always .

member.name: P:System.Windows.Forms.VisualStyles.VisualStyleInformation.ColorScheme
member.summary: Gets the color scheme of the current visual style.

member.name: P:System.Windows.Forms.VisualStyles.VisualStyleInformation.Size
member.summary: Gets the size of the current visual style.

member.name: P:System.Windows.Forms.VisualStyles.VisualStyleInformation.DisplayName
member.summary: Gets the display name of the current visual style.
member.remarks: Reading the active GTK theme name requires an initialized GTK toolkit; to keep this property safe to call at any time (including before a window exists), it returns an empty string rather than probing Gtk.Settings.

member.name: P:System.Windows.Forms.VisualStyles.VisualStyleInformation.Company
member.summary: Gets the company that created the current visual style.

member.name: P:System.Windows.Forms.VisualStyles.VisualStyleInformation.Author
member.summary: Gets the author of the current visual style.

member.name: P:System.Windows.Forms.VisualStyles.VisualStyleInformation.Copyright
member.summary: Gets the copyright information for the current visual style.

member.name: P:System.Windows.Forms.VisualStyles.VisualStyleInformation.Url
member.summary: Gets the URL supplied by the author of the current visual style.

member.name: P:System.Windows.Forms.VisualStyles.VisualStyleInformation.Version
member.summary: Gets the version of the current visual style.

member.name: P:System.Windows.Forms.VisualStyles.VisualStyleInformation.Description
member.summary: Gets the description of the current visual style.

member.name: P:System.Windows.Forms.VisualStyles.VisualStyleInformation.SupportsFlatMenus
member.summary: Gets a value indicating whether the current visual style supports flat menus. Always .

member.name: P:System.Windows.Forms.VisualStyles.VisualStyleInformation.MinimumColorDepth
member.summary: Gets the minimum color depth supported by the current visual style.

member.name: P:System.Windows.Forms.VisualStyles.VisualStyleInformation.TextControlBorder
member.summary: Gets the color that the current visual style uses to draw a text-control border.

member.name: P:System.Windows.Forms.VisualStyles.VisualStyleInformation.ControlHighlightHot
member.summary: Gets the color that the current visual style uses to draw highlighted, hot-tracked controls.

member.name: T:System.Windows.Forms.VisualStyles.VisualStyleRenderer
member.summary: Provides methods for drawing and obtaining information about a .
member.remarks: On this GTK layer there is no Windows theme service to query, so the drawing methods fall back to classic rendering (via and ) and the Get* query methods return sensible defaults. The class/part/state triple is tracked so source that inspects it behaves.

member.name: T:System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis.DynamicallyAccessedMembersAttribute
member.summary: Indicates that certain members on a specified are accessed dynamically, for example through .
member.remarks:
This allows tools to understand which members are being accessed during the execution of a program.
This attribute is valid on members whose type is or .
When this attribute is applied to a location of type , the assumption is that the string represents a fully qualified type name.
When this attribute is applied to a class, interface, or struct, the members specified can be accessed dynamically on instances returned from calling on instances of that class, interface, or struct.
If the attribute is applied to a method it's treated as a special case and it implies the attribute should be applied to the "this" parameter of the method. As such the attribute should only be used on instance methods of types assignable to System.Type (or string, but no methods will use it there).

member.summary: PrintDocument defines a reusable object that sends output to a printer. member.name: T:System.Drawing.Printing.PrinterSettings
member.summary: The nested capability-collection types (, , and installed printers) that a printer exposes. They were absent, so code enumerating a printer's capabilities did not compile. With no print system behind the shim the collections are empty, consistent with the virtual-device defaults documented in EMULATION-GAPS.md.
Represents the settings of a printer, including page ranges, copies and device-specific information. This is a lightweight, cross-platform implementation used by the GTK-based windows-forms shim.

member.name: T:System.Resources.ResXFileRef
member.summary: Converter is a class that is used to convert a ResXFileRef object to and from a string. The string format is "fileName;typeName;[encoding]". The fileName is the name of the file that is being referenced, the typeName is the name of the type that is being created from the file, and the encoding is the encoding of the file (optional, only used for text files). The Converter class is used by the ResXResourceWriter class to write resources to a .resx file, and by the ResXResourceReader class to read resources from a .resx file.
